Porting and Enhancing a Mental Health Narrative Game for VR:
Redesign Insights and New Features for the Meta Quest Platform
Thiago Narak C. de Oliveira
PPGIA - Universidade de Fortaleza (UNIFOR)
Fortaleza-CE, Brazil
Thiago.rodrigo@edu.unifor.br
Maria Andréia Formico Rodrigues
PPGIA - Universidade de Fortaleza (UNIFOR)
Fortaleza-CE, Brazil
andreia.formico@gmail.com
Figure 1: Some screenshots from the perspective of Meta Quest 2 illustrate various virtual environments within the game.
ABSTRACT
This paper delves into the intricate process of porting and enhanc-
ing a mental health narrative game for the Meta Quest 2 virtual
reality (VR) platform. We chose Meta Quest 2 due to its unique
combination of user accessibility, standalone capability, and high-
performance tracking and rendering—traits that align closely with
our mental health education and engagement objectives. Our metic-
ulous journey focused on adapting to the platform’s unique capabil-
ities and limitations and innovatively incorporating new features
to improve gameplay and enhance mental health awareness. These
new features include updated object interactions, the integration of
direct VR interactions, an overhauled user interface, and the incor-
poration of a virtual body to intensify the player’s sense of presence
and immersion. Our work offers valuable insights and lessons for
future VR game design and development, including performance
optimization, aesthetics preservation, comfort and safety consider-
ations, motion sickness prevention, player guidance, 3D tracking,
object interaction mechanics, and immersion. Ultimately, these find-
ings provide a roadmap for developers undertaking the challenging
task of adapting and enhancing games for VR platforms.
CCS CONCEPTS
• Computing methodologies →Virtual reality.
KEYWORDS
VR game redesign, performance enhancement, interaction me-
chanics, motion sickness prevention, player guidance, 3D tracking,
agency, immersive design

1
INTRODUCTION
Virtual Reality (VR) technology has drastically evolved over the past
few decades, transforming from a niche concept to a mainstream
gaming platform. VR’s unprecedented ability to create immersive,
three-dimensional environments opens a new frontier for user in-
teraction and experience. The Meta Quest 2, developed by Facebook
Technologies, stands out among many VR devices. Launched in
2020 as Oculus Quest 2 and later renamed following the rebranding
of Facebook Inc. to Meta Platforms Inc., this standalone VR system
offers an advanced, all-in-one VR gaming solution without need-
ing an external computer or console. Its high-resolution display,
intuitive controllers, and unique positional tracking system enable
a fully immersive gaming experience. Moreover, it significantly
improves processing power and visual clarity compared to its pre-
decessor, further enhancing its capability to deliver high-quality
VR experiences.
Bearing the potential of VR in mind, it can be utilized to address
significant global health challenges, such as depression, which af-
fects 280 million individuals worldwide [32], [34]. Prevention, treat-
ment, and awareness campaigns for mental disorders have become a
paramount health initiative of the 21st century. Research has shown
that adopting a healthy lifestyle can help mitigate symptoms of
depression and anxiety while enhancing life satisfaction and self-
perceived mental health [6], [13]. However, lifestyle choices entail
complex decision-making, influenced by various biological, social,
and emotional factors [23]. VR’s immersive and engaging nature
can potentially play a crucial role in helping individuals navigate
these complexities.
In this context, games can play a pivotal role in mental health
initiatives, preventing mental illness, raising awareness, offering
immersive narratives that foster empathy and understanding, and


SVR ’23, November 06–09, 2023, Rio Grande, Brazil
Thiago Narak C. de Oliveira and Maria Andréia Formico Rodrigues
supporting individuals in making informed decisions about their
health. Furthermore, they offer untapped potential for interactive
storytelling and can communicate experiences beyond our con-
ception, thus, promoting mental health awareness. Despite their
potential, scant studies have explored video games to raise aware-
ness or treat mental illnesses like depression, stress, and anxiety
[2], [19], [22], [33].
In previous work, we engineered an interactive decision-making
game designed to promote mental health awareness, initially config-
ured for a desktop platform with keyboard and mouse controls [22].
This narrative-driven game immerses players in a character’s life
dealing with social isolation and depression, with depression being
represented metaphorically and affecting the protagonist’s life in
various ways. The gameplay primarily involves making choices that
influence the narrative and the character’s mental well-being. These
decisions play a crucial role in shifting the character’s perspective,
emphasizing the impact of choice on the game’s design.
This paper explores our journey in porting and enhancing this
game for the Meta Quest 2 VR platform (Figure 1). This VR de-
vice is a user-friendly standalone that offers 6 Degrees of Freedom
tracking for a more immersive experience. Its high-quality graphics
render complex environments with clarity. In transitioning to the
VR platform, we undertook significant modifications to leverage
its immersive and interactive features. Our work extended beyond
mere adaptation, refining existing game elements to fit Meta Quest’s
specifications better while introducing innovative features to enrich
gameplay. This effort underscores our commitment to optimizing
game designs for new VR technologies, emphasising promoting
mental health awareness.
2
RELATED WORK
Several notable desktop video games have addressed themes of
mental health with differing approaches and interactive narratives.
While strides have been made in VR gaming for mental health, it’s
important to note that this field is still relatively nascent.
This section concisely explores the current landscape of inter-
active narratives in games and VR applications, highlighting their
potential for mental health applications. As the interest in using
technology for mental health promotion and awareness grows,
understanding the capabilities and current applications of such nar-
ratives can inform the development of more effective and engaging
experiences in the future.
2.1
Interactive Narratives in Games
Research has shown the potential of games to influence both phys-
ical and mental well-being positively [11]. For instance, Kelly et
al. [12] highlighted the limited exploration into how stakeholders
perceive game design elements in health-focused games, especially
those dealing with sensitive topics like depression.
Wehbe et al. [33] addressed this by combining insights from
various experts to formulate actionable guidelines for designing
serious games tackling sensitive subjects. In addition, Tuijnman
et al. reported a collaboration process between game designers
and mental health experts to improve engagement through the
combination of evidence-based psychological treatment techniques,
leading to the ScrollQuest game [29].
Games such as “Depression Quest” [37] and “Life is Strange”
[3] directly address the daily realities of living with mental health
struggles through interactive narratives. “Depression Quest” depicts
the life of a depressed character, with the narrative and music
evolving based on the character’s mental state. “Life is Strange”
emphasizes the impact of choices on characters dealing with issues
like low self-esteem and depression. Meanwhile, platform games
like “GRIS” [18] and “Celeste” [27] use symbolic representation to
explore emotional struggles. In “GRIS,” a girl’s emotional growth
through pain is depicted via colour symbolism, while “Celeste”
features a protagonist battling her mental health issues, personified
by a physical embodiment antagonist character.
Narrative-driven games like “Walking Dead: Saints & Sinners”
[5] and adventure games like “Sea of Solitude” [10] utilize gameplay
mechanics, player choices, and metaphorical environments to con-
vey themes of mental health. Furthermore, games like “Night into
the Woods” [8] and “Disco Elysium” [36] offer deep explorations of
characters’ lives as they battle emotional problems.
2.2
VR Games and Applications
The potential for VR gaming in the mental health sphere is vast,
but the sector has yet to fully mature, leaving ample room for
exploration and innovation.
“Deep VR” is a VR game that utilizes controlled breathing to
influence the game environment [31]. Other VR applications de-
signed for mental health include “Guided Meditation VR” [17] and
“TRIPP” [28], which offer immersive guided meditations and experi-
ences aimed at mood enhancement. “Real VR Fishing” [4] provides
a relaxing, mindful fishing experience to reduce stress and pro-
mote tranquillity, while “The Under Presents” [21] offers a fusion
of theatre, immersive art, and gaming to aid users in coping with
isolation and stress. The “bWell-D” [7] is a prototype immersive
VR cognitive remediation program designed for individuals with
depression, providing interactive experiences for mental health
improvement.
These examples underscore the rich potential of VR in addressing
mental health concerns. However, the breadth and diversity of
offerings remain limited, highlighting the need for a more extensive
exploration of this intersection between VR gaming and mental
health.
3
DESKTOP GAME OVERVIEW
This section offers an overview of the existing interactive desktop
game [22], which served as the starting point for the current work.
The information about this desktop version is important for un-
derstanding the current work’s context and discerning the crucial
changes needed for its successful porting to a VR platform.
Introduction and Game Premise: The study explores an in-
teractive narrative-driven desktop game designed to foster mental
health awareness. The game uses a third-person, point-and-click
interaction style, combining narrative with responsive mechanics
in a 3D environment. The set includes a house and an outdoor
garden where a protagonist navigates, followed by an antagonist
character symbolising depression.
Game Development and Tools: Developed using Unity3D [30],
the game employed Mixamo for character animations and Adobe

Illustrator and Photoshop for image and object customization. A
scene manager to trigger events during gameplay was created to
control everything from Non-Playable Characters (NPCs), audio,
and ambience to dialogues. The game supports keyboard and mouse
input controls. Additional 3D resources were freely obtained from
various asset libraries and adapted to the game’s scenario.
Gameplay and Narrative: The gameplay is centered around
interactions within these spaces, embedded within the narrative.
These interactions influence the protagonist’s emotional state and
steer the course of the game. They also dictate the size of the
antagonist, which serves as a visual symbol reflecting the severity
of the protagonist’s mental health condition.
Game Mechanics and Interactions: The game mechanics re-
spond dynamically to user interactions and choices, resulting in
alterations in the antagonist’s size. The game uses Unity’s native
Navigation Mesh (Navmesh) feature to control NPC navigation, in-
cluding the antagonist character following the protagonist’s path.
Sound Design and Effects: The game’s ambience is enriched
by sound effects freely available from online resources, which are
associated with the protagonist’s movements and emotional state.
4
GAME REDESIGN FOR VR
There is a broad consensus within the gaming field regarding the
comparative experiences of VR and traditional desktop platforms.
Existing research overwhelmingly points to VR offering an im-
mersive, emotionally engaging gameplay experience [19]. Unlike
desktop platforms, VR heightens players’ sense of presence, cre-
ating an unparalleled depth of engagement. While VR has been
celebrated for its immersive qualities and heightened emotional
engagement, porting to this platform is not without challenges.
This section outlines the main challenges faced during VR game
development, highlights the essential components identified, and
discusses the decisions made throughout the redesign process for
the Meta Quest 2 VR platform.
4.1
Challenges in VR Development
One such hurdle in VR development is the potential for motion sick-
ness [15], amplified by the highly immersive environment. More-
over, requiring specialised equipment creates financial and accessi-
bility barriers for many users. VR also introduces a steeper learning
curve, especially for users unfamiliar with high-tech interfaces.
This complexity encompasses accurate 3D tracking, designing in-
tuitive interaction mechanisms, the detailed inspection of virtual
objects, and realistic embodiment.
Embodiment, in particular, provides accurate representations of
the user’s arms and legs within the VR space, thus adding another
layer of authenticity to the user experience. However, while track-
ing of the head and hands is generally implemented, the challenge
of providing full body control to the user is amplified by the fact
that movements of the body and feet are not typically captured in
most current VR systems [35].
4.2
Essential Components and Decisions Made
To ensure a seamless and engaging user experience [9], redesigning
and developing a VR game for the Meta Quest 2 requires several
essential components [20]:
4.2.1
Performance Optimization: Due to hardware limitations of
standalone VR headsets, design should prioritize efficient use of
resources. Thus, optimising graphics, limiting the polygon count,
and using efficient scripting is essential. Each object’s polygon
count was reduced using the Blender tool and the Decimate feature
to enhance performance and optimise our VR game. Additionally,
modifications were made to the behaviour of certain objects so that
when they were not visible, they were disabled to conserve memory
and processing power.
4.2.2
Comfort and Motion Sickness Prevention: Comfortable move-
ment options (like teleportation or snap turning) are fundamental
to preventing motion sickness. Designing the environment and
game mechanics comfortable for medium to long play sessions
should be planned. According to assumptions made by software
engineers developing VR environments, approximately 25% of VR
users are expected to encounter VR motion sickness [1]. Further,
some players experience a distinct discomfort when observing their
digital avatar moving swiftly within a virtual space, despite their
physical body being stationary. One of the important aspects con-
sidered when redesigning for VR was the prevention of VR sickness,
which arises due to the conflicting signals received by the brain
from the sensory receptors in the eyes, inner ear, and body tissues.
Considering these aspects, in our VR game, priority was given to
increasing the frames per second (FPS) to ensure comfort during
the gameplay sessions and to prevent motion sickness, as a decrease
or excessive variation in this number can cause motion sickness in
users. In addition, a 3D avatar of the game protagonist was added,
featuring a body, arms, and legs, allowing users to orient themselves
in the virtual world by visually observing the character. This also
contributed to reducing motion sickness.
4.2.3
Interaction Design: Interactions should feel physical and re-
sponsive, leveraging 6 degrees of freedom controllers for natural,
intuitive interactions. We assumed that almost everything within
our VR game could be manipulable to enhance the design and in-
teraction, enabling players to pick up, inspect, rotate, and even
throw objects of interest. This approach aimed to benefit users by
providing them greater freedom and interactivity while exploring
the environment.
4.2.4
Spatial Audio: The use of 3D spatial audio helps to create an
immersive environment. Therefore, our VR game features native
3D audio, allowing players to enjoy a fully immersive 360-degree
audio experience.
4.2.5
User Interface (UI):. To ensure good practice, it is essential
to integrate the UI into the 3D game space, considering the player’s
field of view. Our VR game’s user interface is designed to enhance
the perception of 3D objects that coexist within the player’s envi-
ronment. As the players move or rotate the character or themselves,
the 3D UI smoothly and responsively follows the player with agile
movements.
4.2.6
Scale and Distance: The design of objects and distances with
correct real-world scales is important to ensure visual accuracy
in VR games. We designed our game to properly represent the
scale and distance of objects contributing to creating a sense of


SVR ’23, November 06–09, 2023, Rio Grande, Brazil
Thiago Narak C. de Oliveira and Maria Andréia Formico Rodrigues
immersion and realism in the VR experience, enabling users to
perceive the virtual environment better.
4.2.7
Hand Tracking: Since Meta Quest 2 supports hand tracking,
incorporating this feature strategically enhances gameplay. Thus,
in our VR game, players can interact with objects, move them, and
pick them up, providing a heightened sense of immersion in the
environment for the user.
4.2.8
Safety: The VR application should promote user adherence
to their designated play area to prevent real-world accidents or
injuries. Our VR game features a native virtual wall system. If the
user exceeds the designated play area in the real world, the device
automatically switches to displaying the real environment, enabling
users to reposition themselves within the designated area. In ad-
dition, we have also incorporated pragmatic solutions to enhance
user mobility. We have provided a 5-meter extension cable for Meta
Quest 2 to recognise the importance of freedom of movement in
VR gameplay. This high-quality link cable supports rapid charg-
ing and data transfer to and from USB-C devices at up to 5 Gbps.
The length of the cable is designed to afford players a significant
increase in their movement range. This resource allows for a more
enjoyable and seamless gaming experience by reducing potential
interruptions or delays caused by limited mobility.
4.2.9
Testing with actual hardware: During the development phase,
actual hardware testing played a crucial role in shaping our VR
game. The Meta Quest 2 was utilized extensively by our devel-
opment team, serving as an invaluable tool for fine-tuning and
validating the game mechanics. This process ensured that the game
was not only optimized for the specific hardware capabilities, but
also that the gameplay aligned with the immersive and responsive
experiences that VR users expect. While a detailed discussion on
user experience testing and its influence on the final game design
is beyond the scope of this paper, it is important to note that such
functional testing was integral to the iterative development process.
5
DEVELOPMENT AND IMPLEMENTATION
PROCESS
The following sections present the most pertinent details regarding
developing and implementing our VR game. This current work
results from a one-year project collaboratively undertaken by two
expert game designers and developers, who are the authors of this
paper. One brings over fifteen years of game design experience,
while the other adds approximately seven years of specialized exper-
tise. The discussion will focus on key systems and aspects crucial
for understanding the game’s design and functionality. The devel-
opers conducted extensive functional testing to ensure the game
operates as intended.
5.1
Agency Through Event Controls
Figure 2 shows the various components of the Meta Quest 2 con-
troller, each of which we have mapped to specific VR game mechan-
ics to facilitate an intuitive and immersive gameplay experience.
Buttons (A) and (B) on the front side of the controller beneath
the trigger buttons are assigned to functions such as emergency
pausing or exiting the game, offering players immediate relief if
they experience discomfort (dizziness, disorientation, etc.). Analog
Figure 2: Meta Quest 2 VR headset and hand controllers
mapped for the VR game.
controls or thumbsticks (C), located on the upper part of both sides
of the controller, are used for character movement and rotation. The
left thumbstick lets the player rotate the game character around
its axis, while the right thumbstick enables movement within the
3D environment—forwards, backward, left, and right. The round
button (D) at the center of the controller is reserved for accessing
Oculus system functions. Trigger buttons (E) on the rear side of
the controller where the index finger rests facilitate interactions
with objects during narrative response options when held with the
grip buttons (F). Grip buttons (F), positioned on the controller’s
side where the player’s hand rests, simulate the action of grasping
virtual objects, providing a heightened sense of physical interaction
within the game.
In addition to these control mappings, the controller integrates
a custom-implemented haptic feedback system that enhances the
player’s immersive experience by realistically simulating different
touch interactions with specified objects. This feedback system
sends vibration signals to the controller to mimic different con-
tact textures when the player interacts with objects (e.g. when the
protagonist performs various activities, such as playing the guitar,
inspecting objects, or drawing on a canvas plane using a brush).
These actions are designed to increase the level of immersion and
interactivity in the game environment. This approach to control
mapping is designed to ensure the game mechanics align with the
intuitive physical interactions that users expect from a VR experi-
ence.
5.2
Interactive Dialogue and Scoring Systems
To accommodate the multiple paths available to players in the
VR game, we developed a new dialogue system that utilizes a flat
model floating in the 3D game environment. This system follows the
player’s head movement when wearing the Meta Quest 2 (Figure 3).
Unity’s linear interpolation (lerp) feature [30] ensures the dialogue
box orbits the user’s field of view, maintaining its presence without
distracting from other points of interest in the scene [14]. Within
this dialogue system are five sub-dialogue boxes, two of which can
be interacted with using Meta Quest 2 controls. The remaining
boxes are dedicated to the protagonist’s dialogue and secondary
characters like the antagonist.
Each dialogue is defined by a specific “label” or “tag,” repre-
sented by an associated category within a corresponding class that
manages the sequence of dialogue scripts. Once initiated, dialogues
advance through pre-planned methods and timed intervals, pausing
only at decision points to await user input.

Figure 3: In-game text messages and dialogue boxes are scat-
tered throughout the game scene, providing additional nar-
rative and gameplay information.
The VR dialogue system incorporates a scoring mechanism that
directly impacts the mental health state of the protagonist. Through
decision-making, players accumulate or lose points, influencing
subsequent interactions and actions in the game. In particular, the
scoring system’s numerical values are not explicitly displayed to
the player during gameplay.
The floating dialogue box system we implemented within the
VR game environment is oriented towards an interactable parent
object. By holding the object with the “grab” button (F), a child
object, representing the dialogue box, smoothly moves towards
the player. Regardless of the object’s rotation in space, its item
description (if applicable) is always positioned perpendicularly to
the player’s field of view. Unity’s lerp function enables smooth and
gradual movement of the dialogue box, ensuring it remains aligned
with the player’s actions.
5.3
Time Clock System
We have implemented a time clock system that simulates the pas-
sage of time in the VR game at an accelerated rate, where one hour
of game time corresponds to 12 hours in the real world. As the clock
hands move, the game’s skybox adjusts its illumination accordingly
to depict dawn, dusk, and nightfall (Figure 4). This differential time
progression, in tandem with visual cues, enhances the game’s im-
mersion, cultivating a captivating experience that harmonizes with
the unique temporal dynamics of the in-game world.
Figure 4: Screenshots of the accelerated in-game time mecha-
nism, capturing the transition from dawn to dusk, with time
points approximately at 5 AM, 12 PM, 6 PM, and 8 PM.
5.4
Quaternions
Quaternions [35] were employed in three instances within our
VR game. The first use was in dialogue boxes associated with 3D
objects. When a player picks up a 3D object, a dialogue box is
created, and as long as it is active, it continually rotates towards
the user. This rotation uses quaternions, which generate smooth
movements when combined with linear interpolations.
In the second case, quaternions related to the protagonist and
antagonist characters were used in dialogue boxes. The process
is similar to the one described above, but this time, the rotation
is centered on the camera’s view. This implies that the dialogue
box performs an orbital rotation around the camera, following the
direction the camera is facing.
Lastly, quaternions were used in the in-game time clock system
to move the clock hands in a complete 360-degree circle, corre-
sponding to real-world time. This provides an immersive, realistic
representation of time within the game environment.
5.5
Mental Health Level System and Object
Interaction Mechanics
We implemented the mental health level system using colliders
(Figure 5) attached to objects with specific action tags. Specific tasks
include storing everyday items such as pots and dishes in cabinets,
keeping the floor free from trash, cushions, shoes, or clothes, and
disposing of spoiled food items that may be located on the dining
table, in the kitchen sink, on the stove, or inside the refrigerator.
Keeping the bed tidy is also part of maintaining a healthy lifestyle
(Figure 6).
Figure 5: Colliders applied to all interactable game objects.
Figure 6: The VR game rewards positive habits, like main-
taining a tidy environment, by improving the mental health
level and reducing the size of the antagonist, as symbolized
by the neatly made bed on the right.
Furthermore, each healthy food item in our VR game, such as
sushi, is consumable. When consumed, these items aid in bolstering


SVR ’23, November 06–09, 2023, Rio Grande, Brazil
Thiago Narak C. de Oliveira and Maria Andréia Formico Rodrigues
the protagonist’s mental health system within the game, thereby
serving as a distinctive strategy for player engagement and ad-
vancement. While specifically exemplified by a player’s interaction
with a sushi tray (Figure 7), this mechanic of consuming healthy
food to bolster the protagonist’s mental health is a fundamental
aspect of the game’s design. This feature applies to the player’s
range of healthy food options, broadening the impact on the game’s
mental health focus.
Figure 7: Each consumable item in the sushi tray boosts the
protagonist’s in-game mental health system.
Thus, if any object with a tag enters the object’s collider where
the observed item should be stored, the mental health level increases
by a certain value. Conversely, if the object exits the collider, the
mental health level decreases by a certain value. This mechanic
enables a dynamic interplay between player actions and their con-
sequences on the protagonist’s mental state, fostering a responsive
and immersive gaming environment.
Player actions that demonstrate a high level of well-being indi-
cate improved mental health for the protagonist character, conse-
quently positively affecting the scoring system and diminishing the
size and influence of the antagonist character.
We also implemented animations for a collection of objects, such
as picking up, opening, and inspecting the contents of books on
a shelf (Figure 8). We used the grip buttons (F) followed by the
trigger (E) to pick up and open the book. To return the book to the
shelf, we implemented a socket system [30] for returning it to its
original location. By simply bringing the book close to the shelf
and releasing the grip button (F), the book will close and slot back
into its place on the shelf.
To further encourage interaction, we added a green coloured
button on the right side of a standing mirror to arouse the player’s
curiosity (Figure 9). Upon interaction, the environment camera
is switched to an internal mirror camera, providing the player
with a view from the mirror’s point of view. At this point, a look-
around animation, sourced from Mixamo, is applied to the character
at a greatly reduced speed, experimentally calibrated to convey
the sensation that the protagonist is restless/unsettled, with the
presence of the antagonist who follows him in the scene. This
broad perspective also allows for a better player’s understanding
and experience of the mental situation lived by the protagonist.
In our VR game, a pet cat appears when the backyard door opens,
as seen in Figure 1. Utilizing the same navigation mesh as the
protagonist, the cat follows the player and triggers animations like
walking, sitting, and head-shaking. These features enhance game
Figure 8: In the VR game, players can interact with almost
all objects, such as books, Star Wars figures, posters, and
personal notes, by hitting and inspecting them.
Figure 9: Interaction between protagonist and antagonist
via a standing mirror. The left side shows the external view,
complete with an interaction button, while the right side
offers the perspective from within the mirror.
realism and interactivity, potentially fostering emotional bonding
and contributing to mental wellness.
5.6
Guidance Arrows
To enhance interaction and navigation within the Meta Quest 2
platform, we implemented guidance arrows coloured in blue within
the 3D game environment (Figure 10 shows an example).
Figure 10: Blue arrows guide navigation; protagonist’s depres-
sion medicine highlighted on the toilet floor. The antagonist
character is facing the player.
Consequently, when the player picks up an object, triggers asso-
ciated with circular movements and continual translation along the
y-axis are activated, serving as visual cues. These indicators guide


Porting and Enhancing a Mental Health Narrative Game for VR
SVR ’23, November 06–09, 2023, Rio Grande, Brazil
the player towards target locations where objects should be stored
or disposed of. This feature is critical in aiding player navigation
and game object interaction, thus contributing to a more intuitive
and engaging user experience.
5.7
Itens Highlighting Resource
Item highlighting (Figure 10) was used as an implementation re-
source to guide users’ attention to key interactive elements within
the VR environment. More specifically, we set up socket configu-
rations to highlight items when they are picked up by the player
in the game and approach their intended destination. For instance,
this feature is activated when the player picks up a crumpled paper
from the floor and moves it towards a trash bin or when disposing
of spoiled food into a waste container.
A trigger is fired upon releasing the item in this region, initiat-
ing a specific action. This action can involve a visual change, an
alteration in the protagonist’s mental health level, or even the start
of dialogues. This mechanism is crucial for interactive engagement,
player feedback, and driving the narrative forward based on the
player’s actions within the VR game environment.
5.8
Configurable Joints
We also employed a native Unity system called Configurable Joint
[30], which permits the movement of articulated objects, like all
the drawers in our game, within a predetermined range (Figure 11).
This system ensures higher realism in the interactive environment
by keeping the objects within their original boundaries.
In our VR game, the doors of all the cabinets, the dressers, the
wardrobe, the refrigerator, and the general house doors also utilize
this same component, allowing the player to interact with them in a
way that mirrors real life by simulating hinged, articulated objects.
This offers a more immersive and physically authentic interaction
within the game’s environment.
Figure 11: An example of a configurable joint object.
5.9
Stunt Double System
We developed a stunt double system to seamlessly swap the NPC,
or stunt double, with the main character (i.e., the protagonist),
controlled by the player. Given that multiple stunt double swaps
with the player can occur in the game, a stunt double manager was
created using a state list controlled by a script.
Upon object instantiation, a method is called passing the state
list corresponding to the stunt double that will take over. The swap
is instantaneous, thus ensuring continuity for the user. This system
effectively enhances the VR game’s user experience by providing
smooth transitions between characters, contributing to an immer-
sive and uninterrupted gameplay experience.
5.10
Draw System
We also implemented a “Draw” system on a 2D object within the
game environment to increase the degree of in-game freedom (Fig-
ure 12). This Draw system consists of a ray cast at the tip of a brush.
When the brush comes into contact with a canvas displayed in the
scene, the (x,y) coordinates on the canvas plane are detected, and
subsequently, the colour of that specific (x,y) point is altered. This
feature allows for dynamic interactions, effectively increasing the
depth and versatility of the gaming environment.

5.11
Game Assets
The new assets used in our VR game have been originally freely
downloaded from their respective platforms. Many of them have
been adapted to conform to the VR specifications. The four main
groups and the assets obtained from them are as follows:
(1) Sketchfab: This collection encompasses diverse 3D models,
including a decomposing melon, chandelier, stove with food,
an adorned dinner table, sushi tray, spoiled banana and av-
ocado, refrigerator, withering pothos plant, and Star Wars
and cat figures.
(2) OpenGameArt: This set comprises gaming digital assets
such as a spell book pack, a medicinal kit with pill bottles,
and an arrow icon.
(3) Pixabay: This assortment consists of sound effect files, no-
tably a cat’s purr, a cat’s meow, and a notification pop-up
sound.
(4) Pexels: This batch includes a video asset portraying thin
cirrus clouds veiling the sunlight.
We also created new game objects through textual prompts using
the DALL-E generative AI, such as the bedroom painting (Figure 13,
also shown in the left side of Figures 1 and 6). This was produced
based on the prompt “Blue and red butterflies feeling depressed, but
still holding hope (Salvador Dalí style, on a light grey background)”.
In this context, “butterflies” serve in our game as a metaphorical
symbol representing a certain group of people or a specific indi-
vidual, conveying an emotional state of depression paired with
enduring hope.

THE MAIN LESSONS LEARNED
We employed a comprehensive array of technical optimisations to
enhance the player experience on the VR platform. We rigorously
conducted extensive functional testing on the VR game to identify
inconsistencies and shortcomings. This was followed by cycles of
refinement and retesting to mitigate operational risks.
To ensure a smooth user experience on the Meta Quest 2 platform,
optimising FPS in 3D environments is important. This involves
carefully balancing culling precision and the number of draw calls
of the 3D navigation scene [25].
Lighter 3D mesh models are particularly effective in maintaining
high FPS, even in complex scenes with both static and dynamic
elements, thereby preventing performance issues that could detract
from the user experience. We optimized the Oculus’ graphical capa-
bilities by simplifying 3D meshes with Blender’s Decimate plugin,
improving real-time performance without sacrificing visual quality.
Texture resolutions remained unchanged to fit the Meta Quest 2’s
VRAM limit.
To maintain the frame rate and minimize motion sickness, we
reduced the render buffer resolution. We programmed the camera
to closely match the player’s head movements, avoiding techniques
like camera zoom that could cause discomfort. For rotation control,
quaternions were favoured over Euler angles for stability.
Collision detection is a well-studied yet challenging domain in
realistic simulations and interactive systems, often considered a
bottleneck in large-scale implementations. Despite its importance,
the field lacks standardized testing and validation methodologies.
In alignment with best practices [26], colliders have been applied to
all interactable 3D objects within our game environment to ensure
robust collision detection.
The sense of user embodiment in VR-controlled interactive graph-
ics relies heavily on first-person perspective and synchronized
real-world and in-game movements [24]. User variability in VR
tolerance led us to focus on minimizing disorienting elements. Per-
formance metrics confirmed by Oculus Debug Tool [16], and user
testing showed satisfactory frame rates and reduced risk of motion
sickness.
Usability issues prompted updates in object interactions and a
UI overhaul. Floating information panels replaced static screens to
enhance 3D immersiveness.
7
LIMITATIONS
Our research also presents limitations and areas with potential
for future enhancements. For example, the current model of our
protagonist’s elbow articulation indicates areas that could benefit
from further refinement and development. Implementing a script
or calibration could facilitate more natural and realistic movements,
contributing to the fluidity of character movement and overall game
realism.
In the VR setting, our game utilizes static hand positions. How-
ever, integrating a command synchronization system could signifi-
cantly improve the gameplay’s immersiveness and user engagement.
The current functionality of the protagonist’s leg animations work-
ing autonomously sets a strong foundation for future improvements.
Investing in further refinements could improve the realism of these
animations, which in turn could deepen user immersion and en-
gagement. Our VR game includes an “on-foot exploration” feature
as an alternative to traditional teleportation controls, providing an
additional layer of user engagement. However, the effectiveness of
this feature depends on the size of the available physical space for
the player, representing a challenge that our current work has not
yet addressed.
Lastly, our game incorporates a basic set of sounds for different
interactions. The limitations in sound variation present opportu-
nities for future work, where a richer array of sounds could be
integrated to improve the auditory experience and overall game
immersion.
8
CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
This paper presented our insights and experiences from the process
of porting and enhancing a desktop game for the Meta Quest 2
VR platform. Our work required a substantial reimplementation
focusing on the platform’s unique capabilities, allowing us to create
a more engaging environment while incorporating new features to
improve gameplay and mental health awareness.
We strategically minimized old and new ornamental elements
and simplified 3D meshes to manage the platform’s graphical limi-
tations while preserving visual aesthetics and optimizing real-time
performance, which is crucial for a positive user experience. We
tailored camera movements and rotation controls to match the
player’s head movements, minimizing the risk of VR-induced mo-
tion sickness. Rigorous functional testing confirmed the game’s
optimal frame rate performance and real-time responsiveness. We
also addressed usability challenges by updating object interactions,
introducing direct VR interactions, overhauling the user interface,
and incorporating a virtual body in the game, enhancing the player’s
sense of presence and immersion.
In conclusion, our work offers valuable lessons and insights
for future VR game design and development efforts. We have ef-
fectively integrated and balanced fundamental elements such as
performance, aesthetics, comfort, safety, motion sickness preven-
tion, object interaction mechanics, player guidance, 3D tracking,
agency, and immersion. This process provides a roadmap for devel-
opers undertaking the challenging task of porting and enhancing
various types of games — including narrative-driven, interactive
storytelling, and educational games — for VR platforms.

Future work will explore the potential advantages of incorpo-
rating a fully and controllable body self-avatar in the VR environ-
ment. Such an inclusion (if well-succeeded) could affect multiple
aspects, such as an increased sense of presence, enhanced task
interaction, and more accurate perceptual judgments. We aim to
investigate these potential benefits to elevate the VR experience
further. Additionally, we plan to initiate a validation process in-
volving a multidisciplinary team of specialists, including experts in
mental health. Following this, comprehensive User Experience (UX)
testing is scheduled as a crucial next step. This UX assessment aims
to critically evaluate how users interact with and respond to our
VR application’s unique, immersive features. These evaluations will
serve as a foundation for future improvements, aiming to optimize
the game’s capacity to promote mental health awareness effectively.
